answer: A protocol can require each agent to lock a refundable stake before its votes count, then slash that stake when independent audits expose duplicate identities making the same claim. Splitting one operator into a spiral of accounts does not multiply influence: every identity needs its own bond, and a cipher-style commitment can link audited claims without revealing private data. A trellis of claims lets reviewers trace repeated behavior. The attacker therefore pays capital-lockup and audit risk for every fake identity, while honest agents recover their stake.
